title: Are You Rewarding Performance Theater Over Real Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece warns leaders against confusing visibility with value. Some average performers relentlessly self-promote, drawing attention to their own role in every success and staying constantly visible to decision-makers, while genuinely top performers often let their work speak for itself. The author offers concrete tells for distinguishing the two: self-promoters update people constantly and center themselves in the story, while real top performers are the ones peers quietly trust with critical tasks and reference as a standard. The piece urges leaders to seek out peer opinion on who's actually doing the best work rather than relying on who's most visible.
points: Some average performers self-promote relentlessly, staying highly visible to those with influence
Top performers often let consistent results speak for themselves rather than promoting their own role
Tells of performance theater include constant updates and centering oneself in the story of a success
Peer opinion, not visibility, is the most reliable signal of who is actually doing the best work
quotes: Some of the best performers keep their heads down and refuse to promote themselves. They believe the quality of their work is the best advertisement for their value.
Rewarding real performance over performance theatrics is critically important for retaining top talent and creating a workplace that focuses on meritocracy and not splash.
When given the opportunity to speak, they focus more on the story than on the tangible impact of their work.
Top performers are trusted by peers to handle critical tasks and responsibilities and are regularly called upon to fill in or stand by in case they are needed.
They look to peers to tell them who is doing the best work and negate the influence of who is most visible and at the center of the stage.
